postgres.title: Postgres & query planning
sections:
## Reading an EXPLAIN plan properly

Most people read `EXPLAIN` output top to bottom. That's backwards — the plan is a tree, and execution starts at the leaves.

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
```

The numbers that matter are `actual rows` against `rows` — the planner's estimate. When those diverge by an order of magnitude, everything above that node is built on a bad guess. Fix the estimate before you touch the query.

`BUFFERS` is the other half of the picture: it tells you whether you paid for those rows from shared memory or from disk.

## Why your index isn't being used

The planner isn't ignoring your index out of spite. It has a cost model, and by that model a sequential scan is genuinely cheaper.

Common causes, roughly in order of how often I see them:

1. **Type mismatch** — a `bigint` column compared against a literal the planner treats as `numeric`
2. **Function on the column** — `WHERE lower(email) = $1` cannot use an index on `email`
3. **Low selectivity** — the index matches 40% of the table, so a scan wins
4. **Stale statistics** — `ANALYZE` hasn't run since the data shape changed

The third one isn't a bug. If you're returning most of the table, the index is genuine overhead.

## Partial indexes are underused

If your queries always filter on a status column, you're indexing a lot of rows you never look up.

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_pending
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';
```

On a table where 3% of rows are pending, this index is a fraction of the size of the full one, stays in cache, and gets updated far less often on write. The catch is that the planner only uses it when it can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate — so `WHERE status = 'pending'` works, and a parameterised `WHERE status = $1` does not.

## Connection pooling and the numbers nobody checks

Postgres allocates a process per connection. A few hundred idle connections is not free — it's memory and scheduler pressure for work nobody is doing.

The usual mistake is sizing the pool to peak concurrency. Start instead from how many queries can genuinely run in parallel, which is bounded by cores and disk, not by how many application instances you happen to be running.

> A pool of 20 connections serving 200 application threads is usually faster than 200 connections, because the database stops thrashing.

If you're running serverless, put a pooler in front. Otherwise every cold start opens a connection you'll pay for.

## `NULL` semantics will eventually bite you

Three-valued logic is correct and deeply unintuitive.

```sql
-- Returns nothing, ever
SELECT * FROM products WHERE discount = NULL;

-- What you meant
SELECT * FROM products WHERE discount IS NULL;
```

The subtler case is `NOT IN` against a subquery containing a `NULL`: the entire result collapses to empty, silently, with no error. `NOT EXISTS` doesn't have this problem and usually plans better anyway.

Unique constraints treat `NULL`s as distinct, so you can insert as many rows with a `NULL` in a unique column as you like. That is standard-compliant and almost never what the schema author intended.

## When to reach for a materialised view

Materialised views are a cache with SQL syntax, and they should be evaluated like a cache: what's the staleness budget, and what invalidates it?

They're a good fit when the underlying query is expensive, the data changes on a schedule rather than continuously, and consumers can tolerate lag measured in minutes.

```sql
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY product_stats;
```

`CONCURRENTLY` avoids taking an exclusive lock, but requires a unique index on the view and does more total work. Without it, every reader blocks for the duration of the refresh — which is fine at 3am and very much not fine at noon.

frontend-arch.title: Frontend architecture
sections:
## The rendering strategy is an architectural decision

Server rendering, static generation, and client rendering aren't interchangeable settings. Each one moves work to a different place and makes a different thing hard.

Static generation makes content changes a build problem. Server rendering makes traffic a compute cost. Client rendering makes the first paint a network problem and the second one free.

The question that resolves it is not "which is fastest" but **what changes, and how often**. A pricing page and a dashboard have nothing in common architecturally even though both are pages in the same app.

## Bundle size is a symptom, not the disease

Everyone tracks bundle size because it's easy to measure. It correlates with the thing that matters — time to interactive — but the correlation is loose enough to mislead.

A 400KB bundle that streams and hydrates progressively can beat a 200KB one that blocks on a single synchronous chunk. What actually costs you is:

- **Parse and compile time**, which scales with bytes but worse on low-end devices
- **Main-thread blocking** during hydration
- **Waterfalls** where each chunk request depends on the previous one resolving

Measure the third one first. It's usually the largest and the easiest to fix.

## State that doesn't belong in a state library

A great deal of what gets pushed into global state isn't application state at all.

URL state — filters, pagination, the selected tab — belongs in the URL, where it's shareable, restorable, and survives a refresh for free. Server state belongs in a cache keyed by request, with its own staleness rules. Form state belongs in the form until it's submitted.

What's left over — genuine cross-cutting client state — is usually small enough that the argument about which library to use stops mattering.

## Accessibility failures are mostly structural

The audit findings people get are usually contrast ratios and missing alt text, because those are what automated tooling can detect. Those aren't the failures that stop someone using the product.

The structural ones are: focus that goes nowhere after a modal closes, custom controls that respond to click but not to Enter, live regions that announce every keystroke, and heading levels chosen for their font size.

None of these are caught by a linter. All of them are caught in about ten minutes by unplugging the mouse and trying to complete one task.

distributed.title: Distributed systems
sections:
## Idempotency is a design constraint

Any operation that crosses a network boundary will be retried. Not might — will. The client times out, the proxy retries, the queue redelivers.

This means the interesting question isn't whether to handle duplicates but where the deduplication key comes from. Generated server-side, it can't help you — the retry arrives with a different key. It has to come from the caller.

```http
POST /api/orders
Idempotency-Key: 8f14e45f-ea8b-4c2d-9a3b-1c7d2e5f6a90
```

Store the key with the result, return the stored result on a repeat. The hard part is deciding how long to keep it.

## At-least-once is what you actually have

Exactly-once delivery is not available across a network. What systems offer is at-least-once delivery plus enough machinery on the consumer side to make duplicates harmless.

That machinery is either idempotent operations or a dedup table with a retention window. There isn't a third option, and vendors claiming exactly-once semantics are describing one of these two with better marketing.

> Design for redelivery and the failure modes get boring. Design for exactly-once and you'll discover the exceptions in production.

## Timeouts need budgets, not values

A timeout set per-call is a number someone guessed. A timeout budget is derived: the caller has 3 seconds, spends 200ms on its own work, so the downstream call gets 2.8 seconds minus a margin.

Without budgets you get the classic failure: service A times out at 5s, calls B which times out at 10s. A has already given up and retried while B is still working on the original request, doubling load exactly when the system is struggling.

Propagate the deadline. Most RPC frameworks have a slot for it, and most teams leave it empty.

## Backpressure beats retry storms

When a downstream service slows down, the instinct is to retry. Every caller retrying simultaneously turns a slow service into a dead one.

The mechanisms that actually help:

1. **Circuit breakers** — stop calling a service that's failing, give it room to recover
2. **Jittered exponential backoff** — never retry on a fixed interval, it synchronises callers
3. **Load shedding** — reject early and cheaply when the queue is beyond what you can drain

Shedding load feels like failure. It's the difference between serving 80% of requests and serving none.

## Traces answer the questions logs can't

Logs tell you what one service did. Traces tell you what the request did, which is the thing you're actually debugging.

The investment is in propagation: a trace ID that survives every hop, including the queue, the cron job that picks the message up an hour later, and the third-party webhook. Every boundary where it's dropped is a place where the trace ends and you're back to correlating timestamps by hand.

Sampling decisions should be made at the edge and honoured downstream, otherwise you get partial traces that are worse than none.

## Consistency models are a product decision

"Should this be strongly consistent?" is not an engineering question with an engineering answer. It's a question about what the user is allowed to observe.

A follower count can lag by a minute. A bank balance shown next to a transfer button cannot. Same infrastructure, entirely different requirement, and the cost difference is substantial.

The useful move is to write down the staleness tolerance per read path, in seconds, before choosing a replication strategy. Most teams discover that the majority of their reads tolerate far more lag than the architecture was built to provide.

devex.title: Developer experience
sections:
## The feedback loop is the product

Every internal tool is competing against the developer's willingness to keep using it. That willingness is almost entirely a function of how long they wait to find out if something worked.

A test suite that takes 40 seconds gets run constantly. The same suite at 4 minutes gets run before pushing. At 20 minutes it gets run by CI and nobody else, and the loop has effectively been outsourced.

The threshold isn't linear. There are cliffs — around 10 seconds and around 2 minutes — where behaviour changes qualitatively.

## Local environments should be one command

If onboarding requires a document with more than five steps, that document is out of date. It became out of date the week after it was written and nobody noticed because nobody new joined.

The test is uncomfortable and worth running: hand a laptop to someone who has never seen the repository and watch them try. Don't help. Write down where they get stuck.

Everything they hit is a thing every engineer on the team worked around silently and stopped seeing.

## Error messages are documentation

The error message is read at the exact moment someone needs information, which makes it the highest-leverage documentation surface in the system.

Compare:

```
Error: invalid configuration
```

against:

```
Error: `storage.bucket` is required when `storage.type` is "s3"
  at rebase.json:12
  Set it to your bucket name, or use "type": "local" for development.
```

The second one costs ten extra minutes to write and saves every future reader a search through source. The ratio isn't close.

## Golden paths, not guardrails

A guardrail stops people doing the wrong thing. A golden path makes the right thing the easiest thing. The second scales and the first generates tickets.

When a platform team's main artefact is a list of prohibitions, engineers route around them — not maliciously, but because they have a deadline and the prohibition has no alternative attached.

> If the compliant path is slower than the non-compliant one, you have documented a preference, not established a standard.

## Instrument the tools themselves

Platform teams routinely have no data on their own surface area. Which commands get run, which ones fail, where people abandon a flow — all of it is knowable and almost never collected.

The cheap version is a counter on every CLI subcommand and its exit code. Within a week you learn which command has a 30% failure rate, and it's never the one you'd have guessed.

This is the same argument product teams have accepted for a decade. Internal tools are products with a captive audience, which makes the feedback quieter, not less important.

## Deleting a tool is a feature

Internal tooling accumulates. Every script solved a real problem once, and each one now has a maintenance cost and a probability of being subtly wrong.

The useful discipline is an ownership audit: for each tool, who breaks if it stops working, and who fixes it. Anything with no answer to the second question is already unmaintained — you just haven't found out yet.

Removing it is faster than the incident where someone depends on a thing nobody understands.

typescript.title: TypeScript & type systems
sections:
## `unknown` is the honest version of `any`

`any` disables checking and propagates silently through everything it touches. `unknown` says the same thing — I don't know what this is — while forcing a narrowing step before use.

Every `JSON.parse` result is `any` and should be `unknown`. Every fetch response body is untyped data that you have asserted, not verified. The assertion is a lie the compiler believes.

The fix isn't more type annotations, it's a runtime validation step at the boundary that produces a typed value as its output. Then the type reflects a check that actually happened.

## Generics that get dropped at a seam

A generic parameter is only useful if it survives the whole call chain. When an intermediate function widens it to a base type, everything downstream loses the specificity — and it does so silently, because widening is legal.

This is worth grepping for after any refactor that introduces a wrapper. The symptom is a function that used to reject a wrong field name and now accepts anything, with no error anywhere to indicate the guarantee was lost.

A type-level test — asserting that a known-bad call fails to compile — catches this. Regular tests never will.

## Declaration files are a public API

For a published package, the emitted `.d.ts` is the contract. It's possible for the implementation to be correct and the declarations to be wrong, and consumers only see the second one.

The failure modes are specific: an internal type leaking into a public signature, a re-export that pulls in a dependency's types transitively, or a path alias that resolves locally and nowhere else.

Building the package and typechecking a consumer against the built output — not the source — is the only reliable check. Anything else tests a configuration your users don't have.

## Compile time is a feature you pay for

Type-level programming is genuinely powerful and genuinely expensive. Deeply recursive conditional types can turn a two-second check into a forty-second one, and the cost lands on every developer, on every save.

`--extendedDiagnostics` and `--generateTrace` will tell you which types dominate. It's usually one clever utility applied across a large union.

> The type system is a programming language without a profiler by default. Turn one on before the build time becomes someone's full-time problem.

auth-security.title: Authentication & authorization
sections:
## Authentication and authorization are different problems

Authentication establishes who is calling. Authorization decides what they may do. Conflating them produces systems where being logged in is treated as permission.

The smell is a middleware chain that checks a token and then hands an unrestricted database handle to the route. Every endpoint is now responsible for its own access control, and the one written under deadline pressure won't have it.

Pushing authorization into the data layer — row-level policies, scoped connections — makes the default deny rather than allow.

## Row-level security changes the failure mode

When access rules live in application code, a missing check returns data. When they live in the database, a missing check returns nothing.

```sql
CREATE POLICY orders_select_own ON orders
  FOR SELECT USING (customer_id = rebase.uid());
```

Both are bugs. One is a breach and the other is a support ticket. That asymmetry is the entire argument.

The cost is real: policies are harder to debug, they interact with connection pooling, and an unqualified column reference in a subquery will bind to the wrong table in a way that's easy to miss and hard to spot in review.

## Token lifetime is a tradeoff, not a default

A long-lived access token is convenient and cannot be revoked in any meaningful sense. A short one requires refresh machinery that is itself a source of bugs — races on concurrent refresh, tokens rotated out from under an in-flight request.

The usual shape that works: access tokens measured in minutes, refresh tokens measured in days, rotation on every refresh with reuse detection. If an old refresh token is presented, the family is compromised — revoke all of it.

Getting reuse detection right matters more than the exact lifetimes.

## OAuth goes wrong in predictable places

The protocol is sound. The implementations fail in a small number of recurring ways:

1. **Redirect URI matched by prefix** rather than exactly, which allows an attacker-controlled path
2. **`state` treated as optional**, removing CSRF protection from the callback
3. **Tokens in URL fragments** that end up in browser history and referrer headers
4. **ID token accepted without signature verification**, because it decoded fine

The fourth is the one I find most often. A JWT that parses is not a JWT that's valid, and the base64 payload is readable by anyone.

## Password reset is an authentication flow

It gets treated as a peripheral feature and it is, in practice, a complete account takeover path if it's wrong.

The requirements are the same as login: tokens with short expiry, single use, invalidated on use and on password change. Enumeration matters — the response for a registered and unregistered address must be identical, including timing.

And the reset must invalidate existing sessions. A reset that leaves the attacker's session alive has changed the lock without removing anyone from the building.

## Secrets in environment variables are a floor, not a solution

Moving a credential out of source control is the minimum. It's still readable by every process on the host, it appears in crash dumps, and it's printed by any code that logs its own configuration.

The next step up is a secrets manager with short-lived, automatically rotated credentials, scoped to the workload that needs them. That's a meaningful jump in operational complexity and it's warranted at a smaller scale than most teams assume.

> The question to ask about any secret is: if this leaked today, what would we have to do, and how long would it take?

api-design.title: API design
sections:
## Versioning is about coupling

The REST-versus-RPC argument is usually a proxy for a coupling argument. What matters is how tightly a client is bound to a server's internal model, and how you break that binding when the model changes.

URL versioning is coarse and honest: `/v1` and `/v2` are separate contracts with separate lifecycles and a doubled maintenance cost. Field-level evolution — additive changes, never removing, deprecating with a sunset header — is cheaper but demands discipline that survives staff turnover.

Pick one deliberately. Most APIs end up with both by accident.

## Pagination: offset versus cursor

Offset pagination is easy to implement and wrong under concurrent writes. A row inserted while a client is on page 2 shifts everything, so an item appears twice or not at all.

Cursor pagination encodes a position in the sort order. It's stable under insertion and it scales — `OFFSET 100000` makes the database count a hundred thousand rows to discard them.

The cost is that you lose random access to page N and sort order becomes part of the cursor's contract. For an infinite feed that's no loss. For a table with page numbers it's a UI change.

## Filtering deserves a real grammar

Ad-hoc query parameters accumulate until nobody can enumerate the API's behaviour. `?status=active&min_price=10&created_after=...` grows one parameter per requirement.

An explicit operator grammar is more work initially and bounded thereafter:

```
?where=status:eq:active&where=price:gte:10
```

The important property is that unknown operators are **rejected**, not ignored. Silently dropping a filter the server doesn't understand returns a 200 with wrong data, which is the worst available outcome — the client believes it filtered.

## Partial responses and the N+1 problem

Letting clients specify fields solves overfetching and introduces a new problem: the server can no longer predict its own query shape.

Expansion of related resources is where this turns expensive. `?expand=customer,items.product` looks innocuous and can produce a query per row unless the resolution layer batches.

The defence is a bounded expansion depth, a cap on collection sizes within an expansion, and a query-count assertion in tests. Without the last one, the N+1 comes back with the next feature.

## Idempotency and safe retries

`GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by specification. `POST` is not, and `POST` is where the money moves.

An idempotency key supplied by the client, stored with its response, and replayed on a repeat request turns an unsafe operation into a safe one. The subtleties are in the edges: what happens when the same key arrives with a *different* body (reject), and what happens when the original request is still in flight (conflict, not duplicate).

Document the retention window. A key that expires while a client is still retrying will produce a duplicate charge.

design-systems.title: Design systems & accessibility
sections:
## Tokens are a contract between two teams

A design token isn't a variable — it's an agreement that a value has a name and a meaning, and that both sides will refer to it by that name.

Which is why `blue-500` is a weaker token than `color-action-primary`. The first encodes what it looks like today; the second encodes what it's for, and survives a rebrand.

The generation pipeline matters as much as the naming. If tokens are exported from design tooling by hand, they drift within a quarter. If they're generated, the drift becomes a build failure.

## Component APIs age badly when they mirror design

A `variant="primary-large-icon-left"` prop encodes a specific visual decision into the interface. When design changes, either the name lies or every consumer updates.

Composition holds up better:

```tsx
<Button size="lg" tone="accent">
  <Icon name="plus" />
  Add product
</Button>
```

The orthogonal props compose, and the icon's position is expressed by where it sits rather than by a string. Fewer combinations to document and no invalid ones to guard against.

## Theming needs to survive specificity

A theme applied through CSS variables is only as reliable as the cascade around it. An unlayered global rule beats a utility class regardless of how specific the utility is, which is how a component ends up with a height it never asked for.

```css
/* global.css — wins over any utility */
video { height: auto; }
```

Cascade layers make the precedence explicit and debuggable. Without them, the fix is inline styles, which works and quietly removes the component from the design system's control.

## Focus management is the accessibility work that matters

Automated tools catch contrast and labels. They do not catch what happens to focus when a dialog closes, and that's the thing that strands a keyboard user.

The rules are short:

1. Opening a dialog moves focus into it
2. Focus is trapped while it's open
3. Closing returns focus to whatever opened it
4. Nothing outside is reachable by tab in the meantime

All four are routinely implemented and then broken by a refactor, because nothing tests them. A `focus-visible` assertion in an integration test is cheap insurance.

## Documentation generated from source stays true

Hand-written component docs are accurate on the day they're written. Props get added, defaults change, and the documentation becomes a description of a component that used to exist.

Extracting the prop table from the type definitions, and the examples from files that are themselves typechecked, means the docs fail the build when they're wrong. That's the only mechanism that reliably keeps them current.

The examples matter more than the prop table. Nobody reads the table first.

infrastructure.title: Infrastructure & deployment
sections:
## Most systems don't need Kubernetes

This isn't a criticism of Kubernetes. It's an observation about the operational overhead a team can absorb.

The cluster is not the cost. The cost is the ingress controller, the certificate lifecycle, the network policies, the node upgrades, the CNI behaviour nobody understands, and the on-call rotation to hold all of it.

A single well-provisioned machine with a process manager handles more traffic than most products will ever see, and it fails in ways one person can reason about at 3am.

## Health checks that check nothing

A readiness probe returning `200 OK` from a handler that does no work tells you the HTTP server is running. It does not tell you the instance can serve traffic.

The probe should exercise the dependencies the instance actually needs — a cheap database query, a cache ping — and fail when they're unavailable. Otherwise the orchestrator routes traffic to a pod that will error on every request.

The opposite failure is a probe so thorough it becomes a load source, or one that fails the whole fleet when a non-critical dependency blips. Readiness and liveness want different answers.

## Startup probes exist for a reason

A service with a slow boot — migrations, cache warming, schema validation — gets killed by a liveness probe before it finishes, restarts, and does it again. The result is a crash loop that looks like an application bug and is a configuration one.

`startupProbe` suspends liveness checks until the service reports ready once. It's a few lines of manifest and it's routinely omitted, because everything works fine until the boot sequence gets slower.

The symptom to recognise: restarts that increase under load, when boot takes longer because the database is busy.

## Build pipelines should fail early and loudly

A pipeline where the expensive step runs before the cheap one wastes both time and money on every broken commit.

Order gates by cost: lint, then types, then unit tests, then integration, then build, then deploy. Anything that can fail in 5 seconds should never run after something that takes 5 minutes.

The subtler failure is a pipeline where an early gate failing causes later gates to be *skipped* rather than reported. The run goes red, someone fixes the lint error, and discovers the integration tests were broken too — three commits later.

## Infrastructure cost is an architectural signal

A line item that grows faster than usage is telling you about a design decision. Egress charges that scale with users usually mean assets aren't cached at the edge. Compute that scales with requests rather than with work means something is spinning.

The useful practice is attributing cost per feature rather than per service. It reframes the conversation from "reduce the cloud bill" — which nobody owns — to "this feature costs 40 cents per user per month", which a product manager can act on.

## Rollbacks need to be boring

The deploy that needs rolling back is the one where everyone is stressed and the correct action must be obvious.

That requires: the previous artefact still exists, the rollback is a single command, and migrations applied by the new version are backward compatible with the old one. The third is where it breaks — a column dropped on deploy means the previous version can't run, and you have no rollback, only a forward fix under pressure.

> Expand, migrate, contract. The contract step waits until the rollback window has closed.

data-analytics.title: Data engineering & analytics
sections:
## Model events for the questions you'll ask later

An event captured as `button_clicked` with a label is cheap now and useless in six months. The analysis you'll want is about what the user was trying to do, and the label doesn't carry it.

What makes an event durable is context that can't be reconstructed afterwards: which variant they saw, what state the object was in, where they came from. Anything derivable from other tables can be joined later. Anything ephemeral is lost the moment you don't record it.

Over-capture at write time. Storage is cheaper than a re-instrumentation project.

## Warehouse cost is dominated by a few queries

In every warehouse I've audited, a small number of queries account for most of the spend, and they're almost never the ones anyone worries about.

The usual culprits are a dashboard on a short auto-refresh scanning a large table, and a scheduled job that reprocesses full history nightly because it was easier than incremental.

Both are visible in query logs within an hour of looking. Neither is a modelling problem — they're defaults nobody revisited after the data grew.

## Idempotent pipelines or manual reconciliation

A pipeline that can't be safely re-run is a pipeline that requires a human whenever anything fails. And something fails weekly.

The property to design for is that re-running a window produces the same result as running it once. That usually means writing partitioned output keyed by the window and replacing the partition wholesale, rather than appending.

Append-only pipelines feel simpler until the first backfill, at which point you have duplicates and no way to tell which run produced which row.

## Metrics that change behaviour versus metrics that decorate

Most dashboards are ignored. Not because the numbers are wrong but because no one has ever taken a different action based on them.

The test for a metric worth maintaining: name the decision it informs and the threshold at which the decision changes. A metric with no threshold is a number on a screen, and it costs pipeline maintenance forever.

> Every chart on a dashboard should have someone who would notice if it stopped updating. Most don't.

## Late-arriving data breaks naive aggregation

Events don't arrive in order. Mobile clients buffer while offline and flush days later; a webhook retries for six hours.

Aggregating by arrival time produces numbers that are wrong and *look* right. Aggregating by event time produces numbers that change after the fact, which surprises people reading a dashboard they screenshotted yesterday.

The honest approach is event-time aggregation with an explicit watermark and a stated restatement window — "figures for the last 72 hours may revise" — rather than pretending the problem doesn't exist.

## Slowly changing dimensions, chosen deliberately

When a customer changes their address, does last quarter's revenue report show the old one or the new one? Both answers are defensible and only one matches what finance expects.

Overwriting is simplest and loses history. Versioned rows with validity ranges preserve it and make every join more complicated. Choosing per-dimension rather than adopting one strategy globally is usually right — most attributes don't need history and a few need it absolutely.

The decision is a business one. It gets made by whoever writes the table.

migrations.title: Schema migrations & legacy systems
sections:
## Expand, migrate, contract

A migration that renames a column in one step requires the application and the schema to deploy simultaneously. They won't.

The three-phase version costs more deploys and removes the coordination requirement entirely:

1. **Expand** — add the new column, write to both
2. **Migrate** — backfill, switch reads to the new column
3. **Contract** — stop writing the old one, drop it

Each phase is independently deployable and independently reversible. The contract step can wait weeks; there's no rush and considerable downside to hurrying it.

## Long-running migrations need to be resumable

A backfill that updates ten million rows in a single transaction will hold locks for the duration, bloat the WAL, and fail at 90% because of a timeout you didn't configure.

Batching in chunks of a few thousand, committing between batches, and recording progress somewhere durable turns a 6-hour all-or-nothing operation into something you can stop and restart.

```sql
UPDATE orders SET currency = 'USD'
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM orders WHERE currency IS NULL LIMIT 5000
);
```

Run it in a loop, log the count, sleep between iterations to leave room for production traffic.

## Migration ordering is a trap in team settings

Most migration runners track a high-water mark: the latest version applied. A migration authored on a branch with an earlier timestamp, merged after a later one has run, is silently skipped. Forever.

Nothing errors. The table just doesn't have the column, on production only, and it's discovered weeks later by an exception in an unrelated feature.

The defence is a CI check that the migration sequence in the branch is contiguous with main's, run at merge time rather than deploy time.

## Strangler fig, and when to abandon it

Incrementally routing traffic from an old system to a new one works. What's less discussed is that it produces a period — often years — where both exist and every feature costs double.

The migration succeeds if that period is bounded and someone owns ending it. It fails when the remaining 20% is the hard part, the team moves on, and the strangler becomes permanent architecture.

> Decide up front what evidence would justify stopping. Sunk cost is a strong argument in the room and a bad one on the whiteboard.

## Legacy code is an asset with poor documentation

The system everyone wants to replace is also the system encoding a decade of requirements nobody wrote down. Every strange conditional is a bug report from 2019.

Rewriting from the specification produces something that handles the happy path and fails on the cases the original learned about painfully. That's why rewrites take longer than estimated — the estimate covered the specification, not the accumulated knowledge.

Read the git blame before deleting the branch. It's the only documentation that exists.

## Backward-compatible reads, forward-compatible writes

During any migration there's a window where two versions of the code run against one schema. Getting through it without incident means the old version must tolerate what the new one writes.

Adding a nullable column is safe. Adding an enum value is not — the old version may switch exhaustively and throw on an unknown case. Tightening a constraint is not, because in-flight writes from the old version may violate it.

The general rule: relax constraints before deploying code that relies on them, tighten them only after all writers have been updated.

mobile.title: Mobile & cross-platform
sections:
## Offline-first means conflict resolution

The easy part of offline support is queuing writes. The hard part happens when two devices edited the same record and both come back online.

Last-write-wins is a decision, not a default — it silently discards someone's work. Per-field merging is better for records where fields are independent, and useless for anything with invariants across fields.

What matters most is that the resolution strategy is explicit and testable, and that unresolvable conflicts surface to the user rather than being quietly resolved in favour of whoever synced second.

## Test on the devices people own

The development device is the fastest phone released in the last two years. A meaningful share of users are on hardware three to five years older with a fraction of the memory bandwidth.

Animation that's smooth on the test device drops frames. Startup that takes 800ms takes four seconds. Neither shows up in any metric collected from the team's own phones.

A mid-range device on the desk, used for the final check before merge, catches more real performance problems than any profiling session.

## Cross-platform tradeoffs, honestly assessed

Shared code saves effort on business logic and saves considerably less than advertised on anything touching the platform: navigation, permissions, background execution, push, deep links.

The realistic estimate is that the shared portion is large and the remaining platform-specific portion is where the schedule goes. Teams that budget for 90% shared and hit 70% experience it as a failure; teams that budget for 70% ship on time.

Neither framework choice is wrong. The estimate is what's usually wrong.

## App size affects install conversion

Install completion drops measurably with download size, and the effect is strongest on the connections and devices where your growth is.

The wins are unglamorous: audit bundled assets for things only used in onboarding, check for duplicated dependencies pulled by two libraries at different versions, and confirm image assets are shipped at the resolutions actually rendered.

A 30% reduction is typically available before anyone has to make an architectural change, and nobody looks because size isn't on a dashboard.

## Background work is not guaranteed

Both platforms will kill background tasks, defer scheduled work, and refuse execution based on battery state and user behaviour. Code that assumes a background sync ran is code that will be wrong for a subset of users permanently.

The design consequence: background work is an optimisation, and the foreground path has to be able to catch up from scratch. Anything that only happens in the background eventually doesn't happen for someone, and it fails silently.

Instrument whether the background task ran. Most teams don't know their actual execution rate.

## Push notifications are a delivery-effort system

A push token expires, gets invalidated on reinstall, and is silently dropped when the user has disabled the category. Delivery is best-effort and there's no ack.

Treating a notification as a nudge toward state the server already holds is robust. Treating it as the transport for the state itself means users miss data, and the failure is invisible from the server side.

Token hygiene matters too: feedback from the push service about dead tokens should prune the table, or you'll be paying to send to an audience that uninstalled a year ago.

testing.title: Testing & quality
sections:
## The pyramid is usually an hourglass

The canonical shape is many unit tests, fewer integration tests, a handful of end-to-end. What teams actually have is a large pile of unit tests, a large pile of end-to-end tests, and almost nothing between.

The missing middle is where most real bugs live: the seam between two components that are each individually correct. Unit tests mock across that seam and end-to-end tests are too slow and flaky to cover its permutations.

Integration tests against a real database are the highest-value tests most codebases are missing.

## Flaky tests are a systems problem

A flaky test is treated as an annoyance to retry. It's information: something in the system is timing-dependent, order-dependent, or sharing state it shouldn't.

The retry hides the information and the underlying nondeterminism stays in the product, where it produces bugs that are reported once and never reproduced.

> A suite with a 2% flake rate and 400 tests fails a third of the time for reasons unrelated to the change. At that point the suite has stopped being a signal.

## Test the contract, not the implementation

A test that asserts on internal method calls fails when the implementation is refactored and passes when the behaviour breaks. That's exactly inverted from what a test is for.

The question to ask about each assertion: would this fail if the code were rewritten to be correct in a different way? If yes, it's testing implementation, and it will be deleted during the next refactor by someone who correctly identifies it as noise.

Mock at process boundaries. Inside the boundary, use the real thing.

## Mutation testing finds the tests worth writing

Coverage measures which lines ran. It says nothing about whether a wrong result would have been caught.

Mutation testing changes the code deliberately — flips a comparison, removes a condition — and reports which mutants the suite failed to kill. A surviving mutant is a line that's covered and unasserted.

The output is uncomfortable the first time. It's also the only technique I know that reliably identifies which specific tests are missing rather than telling you a percentage.

## Fixtures drift from reality

A test fixture built two years ago describes an object shape that no longer exists in production. The test passes because both the fixture and the assertion were written against the same wrong model.

This is especially common in test directories excluded from typechecking, where nothing enforces that the fixture matches the current type.

Including tests in the typecheck is a one-line configuration change that immediately surfaces every place a fixture has fossilised. Expect a large number of errors and a genuinely improved suite.

## Contract tests between services

When two services are developed by two teams, integration failures are found at deploy time, which is the most expensive time to find them.

A consumer-driven contract — the caller declares what it needs, the provider's CI verifies it still supplies that — moves the failure to the provider's pull request, where the person who broke it is the person who can fix it.

The organisational effect matters more than the technical one. It relocates the cost of a breaking change onto the team making it.

teams.title: Engineering teams & process
sections:
## Cognitive load is the constraint worth managing

Team size and service count get optimised. What actually limits throughput is how much a team must hold in mind to make a safe change.

A team owning four services in one domain is fine. A team owning four services across four domains, each with its own deployment story and failure modes, is overloaded regardless of headcount.

The symptom is not missed deadlines but caution — changes get slower and smaller because nobody is confident about the blast radius.

## Incident review without blame theatre

"Blameless" is often performed rather than practised. The tell is a review that identifies a human action as the root cause and then adds a process step to prevent it.

The more useful question is why the system permitted the action to have that consequence. Someone ran a command against the wrong environment — why was that possible, why was it not obvious which environment, why did it take eleven minutes to notice?

Action items about attention and care do nothing. Action items about affordances change outcomes.

## Hiring processes filter for interview skill

A process built around algorithmic puzzles selects for people who have recently practised algorithmic puzzles. That's a real skill, correlated weakly with the job.

Work-sample tasks resembling actual work predict better, and cost more to run — someone has to design them and read the results carefully.

The cost is the point. A cheap process that selects poorly is more expensive than an expensive process that selects well, and the bill arrives eighteen months later disguised as a performance problem.

## Code review has a purpose that isn't defect detection

Review catches some bugs, less reliably than tests do. Its durable value is different: it spreads knowledge of the codebase, and it creates a second person who understands why a change was made.

That reframes what a good review is. A comment that improves the code slightly and delays the merge by a day is usually a bad trade. A question that reveals the author and reviewer disagree about how the system works is worth a week.

> Optimise review for shared understanding. Optimise CI for defects.

## Estimates communicate uncertainty or they're noise

A single-number estimate discards the only genuinely useful information: how confident anyone is.

"Three weeks" and "three weeks, unless the third-party API doesn't support bulk updates, in which case six" are different statements. The second lets a planner de-risk by checking the API today.

Estimates get treated as commitments because they're delivered as if there's no uncertainty. Attaching the conditions to the number changes what the conversation is about.

## Career paths that aren't management

When the only route to seniority is managing people, the organisation loses its best engineers to a job they didn't want and may not be suited for.

A credible senior individual-contributor track requires more than a title. It requires the scope to be real — architectural decisions that stick, influence over roadmap, compensation genuinely comparable to the management ladder.

Where those are absent, the track exists on the careers page and nobody is fooled.

performance.title: Performance engineering
sections:
## Measure first, and then measure differently

The first measurement usually confirms what you expected, because you chose what to measure based on what you expected.

The second measurement — a different tool, a different layer, a different time of day — is where the surprises are. A function that dominates a CPU profile may be irrelevant if the request spends 90% of its time waiting on I/O the profiler doesn't show.

Wall-clock time on the actual request path is the ground truth. Everything else is a proxy that's useful right up until it isn't.

## Flame graphs mislead in specific ways

A flame graph shows where CPU time went. It doesn't show time spent blocked, which on most web workloads is the majority.

It also aggregates across samples, so a function that's occasionally catastrophic and usually fine appears as a modest average. Tail latency doesn't show up in a shape optimised for totals.

Use flame graphs to find CPU-bound hot spots, and latency histograms with percentiles to find everything else. The two answer different questions and the second one is more often the one being asked.

## Latency budgets across a request path

A 200ms target for an endpoint means nothing until it's divided. 30ms of network, 20ms of auth, 80ms of database, 40ms of serialisation, 30ms of margin.

With the budget written down, a regression is attributable — the database step went from 80 to 140 and everything else held. Without it, you have a slower endpoint and a debate.

The act of writing the budget is itself informative. Teams routinely discover a step consuming a third of the budget that nobody had considered a cost at all.

## Percentiles, and why the average lies

An average response time of 120ms is compatible with 95% of requests at 50ms and 5% at 1.5 seconds. The average describes no actual user.

p50 tells you the typical experience. p99 tells you what a heavy user hits several times a session — because a page making 20 requests hits the 99th percentile more often than not.

> If your dashboard shows a mean, it's showing you a number that is nobody's experience of the product.

## Caching moves the problem to invalidation

Adding a cache is a few lines. Deciding when it's wrong is the design work, and it never gets easier.

Time-based expiry is simple and serves stale data for the length of the TTL. Event-based invalidation is correct and requires every writer to know about every cache — a coupling that breaks the first time someone writes to the database directly.

The honest position is to state a staleness tolerance per cached value and pick the cheapest mechanism that meets it. Most values tolerate far more than the team's instinct suggests.

## The N+1 that survives the fix

Someone finds a query loop, adds batching, and closes the ticket. Six weeks later a new field is added to the response, resolved per-row, and the N+1 is back with a different shape.

The durable fix isn't the batch loader — it's an assertion on query count in a test covering that endpoint. It fails on the pull request that reintroduces the problem, naming the cause, instead of surfacing as a latency graph three deploys later.

documentation.title: Documentation & developer education
sections:
## Get someone to a working call in five minutes

The quickstart is the only page most people read, and its success criterion is narrow: a request that returns real data, as fast as possible.

Everything that isn't on that path — configuration options, architectural background, the full authentication model — belongs elsewhere. A quickstart that explains concepts before producing a result loses readers at each paragraph.

The measure is literal. Time someone doing it. If it takes twenty minutes, the page is not a quickstart regardless of its title.

## Documentation drift is a testing problem

Every code sample in the docs is an untested assertion about the API. It was true when written and there is no mechanism keeping it true.

Extracting fenced code blocks and typechecking them against the current workspace turns drift into a build failure. It catches renamed exports, changed signatures, and options that no longer exist — the exact failures that make a reader conclude the product is unreliable.

The baseline has to be zero and CI has to enforce it, or the count grows and everyone stops reading it.

## Reference and explanation are different documents

Reference answers "what are the parameters of this function". Explanation answers "why would I use this". Merging them produces a document that's tedious for the reader who wants a lookup and insufficient for the reader who wants to understand.

Reference should be generated from source, because it's mechanical and it drifts. Explanation should be written by a person, because it encodes judgement and it doesn't.

Most documentation problems are a failure to separate these two, and they get diagnosed as a tooling problem.

## Error messages carry more traffic than any doc page

An error is read by someone who is stuck, at the moment they're stuck. No documentation page will ever match that context.

Which means the error deserves the same editorial care as the docs: what happened, what was expected, where, and what to do about it. A link to the relevant page is worth more than a paragraph of prose.

The analytics support this and rarely get consulted — support-ticket volume maps to error text far more tightly than to documentation gaps.

## Write down what the system doesn't do

Documentation describes capabilities. What costs users time is discovering the boundaries — the limit that isn't documented, the combination that isn't supported, the thing that works but not at scale.

An explicit limits page is cheap and prevents a category of support conversation that starts "I assumed". It also forces the team to know its own limits, which is not always the case before someone writes them down.

Being specific about what's out of scope reads as confidence, not weakness.

## Docs architecture is information architecture

When readers can't find things, the usual response is to add a search box or write more pages. Neither fixes a structure that doesn't match how people look.

People arrive with a task, not a topic. Organising by product feature — the way the team thinks — buries the answer under a heading nobody would click.

The cheapest diagnostic is the search log. The queries returning nothing are a list of pages you need, written by your users.

small-teams.title: Small-team engineering
sections:
## Choose boring technology deliberately

Every unfamiliar technology in the stack consumes a portion of a finite budget for things that can surprise you. On a team of three, that budget is very small.

The question isn't whether a new database is better. It's whether it's better by enough to justify being the team that has never operated it, at 2am, with no vendor support and no colleague who's seen this failure before.

Spend the budget where it's differentiating. Use the dullest available option everywhere else.

## Two engineers and no platform team

Advice written for large organisations assumes a platform team exists. Without one, every piece of infrastructure is a thing the product engineers maintain in the time they aren't building product.

That changes the calculus entirely toward managed services, even at a visible premium. The bill is legible; the alternative cost — a founder debugging a certificate renewal on a Saturday — isn't on any invoice but is much larger.

Buy the boring parts. Build only what customers are paying for.

## Ship the ugly version to the people who asked

A feature nobody has used is a hypothesis. Polishing it before validation is spending the expensive resource — engineering time — on the part that might be wrong.

The useful shape is: build the smallest thing that answers the question, give it to the three customers who requested it, watch what they actually do. The gap between requested and used is routinely large.

This only works if you can retract it. Design the smallest version so that removing it is cheap.

## Documentation as a hedge against the bus factor

On a small team, every system has exactly one person who understands it. That's not a process failure, it's arithmetic.

What helps isn't comprehensive documentation, which won't get written. It's a short decision log per system: what we chose, what we rejected, and why. Half a page, written when the decision is fresh.

The successor doesn't need the implementation explained — they can read it. They need to know which constraints were real and which were preferences.

## Generalists by necessity, and it works

Specialisation is efficient at scale and costly below it. When everyone owns a slice, every handoff between slices is a queue, and on a small team the queue is longer than the work.

Engineers who touch the database, the API, the frontend and the deploy pipeline make worse individual decisions in each and much better decisions about the whole. That trade is favourable until roughly the point where a single person can no longer hold the system in their head.

That point arrives later than most teams expect.

## Say no on the record

Small teams die of dilution more often than of any single wrong decision. Each individually reasonable commitment is fine; the aggregate is a team maintaining eleven things and advancing none.

What makes refusal sustainable is writing it down — a visible list of what was declined and why. It converts a series of awkward individual conversations into one strategic position that can be pointed at.

It also lets you revisit honestly when circumstances change, rather than relitigating from memory.

product-eng.title: Product engineering
sections:
## Prototype to answer a question

A prototype built to impress gets polished. A prototype built to answer a question gets thrown away once it's answered, which is the entire point.

Before writing any of it, state the question: will users understand this interaction, is the third-party API fast enough, does this data model support the reports finance needs. The answer determines what to build and — more usefully — what not to.

A prototype without a stated question becomes a foundation by accident, and its shortcuts become architecture.

## Instrument before shipping, not after

The instrumentation added after launch can't answer questions about launch. And launch is when behaviour is most informative, because it's the only time you'll see genuinely first-time use.

Deciding what to measure is also a design exercise: if you can't state what success looks like as a number, the feature's purpose is probably vaguer than the specification suggests.

The conversation is much easier before the code is written than in the retrospective where nobody can tell whether it worked.

## Feature flags need an expiry date

A flag is a temporary branch in the codebase. Left in place, flags multiply the number of possible states, and the combination nobody tested is the one that produces the bug.

The discipline is an owner and a removal date per flag, enforced by something that complains — a lint rule, a scheduled report — rather than by intention.

Without it, a two-year-old flag defaulting to off is dead code that everyone is afraid to remove because they can't prove nothing depends on it.

## The cheapest feature is the one you didn't build

A disproportionate share of engineering effort goes into features that are used by almost nobody, and this is knowable in advance more often than teams admit.

The techniques are unglamorous: a fake door that measures click-through on something that doesn't exist yet, a manual concierge version served by a human for the first ten customers, a hard look at whether the request came from one loud account or from many.

All are cheaper than a quarter of engineering, and all are routinely skipped because they feel like not building.

## Progressive delivery beats a launch date

A feature released to everyone simultaneously has one chance to be right, and any problem is discovered at full blast radius.

Rolling it out by percentage makes the problem small and the rollback boring. It also produces a comparison — the cohort without the feature — which is the only way to know whether the metric moved because of the change or because it was Tuesday.

The cost is that the code must handle both paths for a while. That's usually less work than the incident it prevents.

## Deprecation is a product feature

Removing something is a change to the product, and it deserves the same care as adding one: a notice period, a migration path, a way to tell who is affected.

The part teams skip is the last one. Without usage data per customer, deprecation is either indefinitely postponed out of caution or executed blind and breaks someone important.

> If you can't answer "who is still using this", you can't deprecate it. That's an instrumentation problem, not a policy one.

open-source.title: Open source maintenance
sections:
## Issue triage is the whole job

Writing the library was the fun part and it's over. What determines whether a project survives is whether incoming issues get a response, and that's a sustained obligation with no end date.

Templates help by making reports actionable. Labels help by making the backlog navigable. Neither addresses the actual cost, which is emotional — every open issue is an implied obligation, and the count only goes up.

Closing stale issues honestly, with an explanation, is healthier than an unbounded backlog nobody believes in.

## Semantic versioning is a social contract

The specification is precise about what a major version means. What it can't specify is the judgement call: whether a bug fix that changes observed behaviour is a patch or a break.

Strictly, if anyone depends on the buggy behaviour, fixing it is breaking. Practically, treating every fix as major makes the version number meaningless.

The workable position is to document the intent — what's covered by the compatibility promise and what isn't — so the judgement is at least predictable. Undocumented behaviour is not part of the contract, but only if you said so first.

## Dependency risk compounds quietly

A direct dependency is a decision. Its 40 transitive dependencies are decisions made by someone else, on your behalf, that you will nonetheless own during an incident.

The risk isn't primarily malicious packages, though those exist. It's abandonment — a package with one maintainer who stops, and a security advisory arrives eighteen months later with no upstream fix.

Audit the tree by maintainer count and last release date occasionally. The results are usually worse than expected and identify a small number of genuinely fragile links.

## Unbounded version ranges are not pins

A constraint like `>=2.1.0` written to satisfy a security advisory looks like a floor and behaves like a floating pin. It permits every future major version, including the one that removes the API you use.

The build breaks on a day nobody changed anything, which is the most expensive kind of break because the cause isn't in the diff.

Pin to a range with an upper bound and update deliberately. Lockfiles help and they don't help consumers of a published package, who resolve their own tree.

## Burnout is a maintenance risk

The unpaid maintainer of a widely-used package is a single point of failure, and the failure mode is silent. They don't announce it — the responses just get slower and then stop.

What helps is structural rather than motivational: more than one person with publish rights, documented release procedure, and explicit scope so that requests outside it can be declined without a negotiation each time.

> A project with one maintainer has already failed. The failure just hasn't been observed yet.

## Most good code came from a bug report

The best contributions to a library are usually not features. They're the edge cases someone hit in production and took the time to describe precisely.

That makes the reporting experience worth investing in: a template that asks for a reproduction, a maintainer response that's quick even when the fix isn't, and a changelog that credits the reporter.

The reporters who get that experience come back with the next one. The ones who don't fork the package and fix it privately, and you never learn about the class of bug at all.

ml-retrieval.title: ML engineering & retrieval
sections:
## Retrieval quality is an engineering problem

The attention goes to the model. The thing that determines output quality in most retrieval systems is whether the right documents were fetched, which is a search problem with decades of prior work.

Chunking strategy, hybrid keyword-plus-vector scoring, and metadata filtering move the number substantially. Swapping the embedding model usually moves it less than expected.

Measure retrieval separately from generation. A system evaluated end-to-end hides which half is failing, and the fixes are entirely different.

## Your evaluation set is probably leaking

An eval set assembled from the same source as the training or tuning data reports a number that won't survive contact with production.

The leak is often indirect: examples curated by the same person who tuned the prompts, or sampled from a period whose distribution has since shifted.

A held-out set collected from real traffic, at a different time, labelled by someone who didn't build the system, is worth more than ten times its size assembled conveniently. It will also report a worse number, which is the point.

## Latency budgets for model-backed features

A model call is a network request to a system with variable and occasionally very long response times. Designing around a median is how you end up with a p99 that times out.

The patterns that hold up: streaming so the user sees progress rather than a spinner, a strict deadline with a degraded fallback, and caching for the substantial fraction of requests that are near-identical.

The fallback is the part that gets skipped. A feature with no defined behaviour when the model is slow has defined it implicitly as an error page.

## Prompts are code without a test suite

A prompt edit is a behaviour change deployed with no type checking, no test, and frequently no review. It's the least controlled artefact in the system and it directly determines output.

Treating prompts as versioned artefacts with an eval run attached before merge brings them up to roughly the standard of the rest of the codebase.

The practice that helps most is keeping a regression set of inputs that previously produced bad output. Every prompt change runs against it. Improvements on one dimension routinely regress another, and there's no way to see it otherwise.

## Data plumbing is most of the work

The expectation is model training. The reality is extraction, deduplication, format normalisation, permission handling, and keeping an index in sync with a source that changes continuously.

The sync problem is the one that's routinely underestimated. A document deleted at the source and still present in the index is a correctness and often a compliance issue, and it requires a deletion path that's as reliable as the ingestion path.

Budget the majority of the timeline here. That's not a failure of planning — it's what the work is.

## Be suspicious of any benchmark you didn't build

Published benchmarks measure a task defined by someone else, on a distribution that isn't yours, often with contamination nobody has ruled out.

They're useful for excluding options and nearly useless for choosing between the top few. The gap between benchmark rank and behaviour on a specific workload is routinely large.

A small evaluation set drawn from your own traffic — even a hundred examples, labelled carefully — predicts production quality better than any leaderboard, and can be built in a day.
